# What this document does

This is the R counterpart to the Python/scikit-learn notebook. It builds Naive Bayes
classifiers three times, at increasing scale:

| | Example | Data | Rows | Features | Point of the exercise |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Weather & golf | lecture slides | 14 | 1 categorical | Verify the library reproduces the hand calculation |
| 2 | Voter turnout | lecture slides | 14 | 3 categorical | The independence assumption; the zero-frequency problem |
| 3 | Income & inequality | **real data** — 1994 US Census | ~32,500 | 12 engineered | A full applied workflow and its limits |

**To run this:** open in RStudio and click **Knit**, or run chunks one at a time with
`Ctrl+Shift+Enter`. Example 3 downloads data and needs an internet connection the first
time.

## Dependencies, deliberately few

Almost everything below is base R and `stats`. The only external package is `e1071`,
which provides `naiveBayes()`. Even that is optional: every result is also computed
longhand, so the document knits and teaches with or without it.

```{r deps}
have_e1071 <- requireNamespace("e1071", quietly = TRUE)

if (!have_e1071) {
  cat("e1071 is not installed. Install it with:  install.packages('e1071')\n",
      "The hand-rolled sections below still run and produce every number.\n")
} else {
  library(e1071)
  cat("e1071 version:", as.character(packageVersion("e1071")), "\n")
}

cat("R version:", R.version.string, "\n")
```

## First-run check

Three numbers below are fixed by arithmetic, not by anything version- or
platform-specific. If your run reproduces them, the document is working. If it does not,
something in your setup differs and the rest of the output should not be trusted.

| Where | Quantity | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| 1.3 | `P(Yes | Sunny)` | **0.6000** |
| 2.2 | `P(Yes | Senior, Contacted, High)` | **0.8527** |
| 2.6 | same case as 2.5 with `laplace = 1` | **0.7523** |

The two `stopifnot()` self-tests on the AUC helper in section 3.5 serve the same purpose
for Example 3: if either fails, knitting stops there rather than producing plausible
nonsense.

## Which R function should you use?

| Function | Package | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `naiveBayes()` | `e1071` | The workhorse. Gaussian for numeric predictors, categorical for factors, chosen automatically per column. |
| `naive_bayes()` | `naivebayes` | Newer, more explicit control (`usekernel`, `usepoisson`), nicer `tables()` accessor. |
| `NaiveBayes()` | `klaR` | Adds kernel density estimation for numeric predictors. |
| via `discrim` | `tidymodels` | If you are already working in a tidymodels pipeline. |

We use `e1071` because it is the most widely installed and the least ceremonious.

## Three R-specific traps, stated before we hit them

These bite people in R specifically, and two of them are silent.

1. **`stringsAsFactors` defaults to `FALSE` since R 4.0.** `read.csv()` gives you
   *character* columns, not factors. `naiveBayes()` needs factors to treat a variable as
   categorical. Forget to convert and your carefully categorical model may not be one.
2. **Numeric columns get a Gaussian automatically.** There is no separate `CategoricalNB`
   / `GaussianNB` choice as in Python — `naiveBayes()` inspects each column and decides.
   So an integer-coded category (`1, 2, 3` for education level) is silently fitted with a
   normal distribution, implying those codes sit on a number line. Same error as in Python,
   but easier to make here because nothing in the function call reveals the assumption.
3. **`e1071` has two smoothing mechanisms, not one.** `naiveBayes(laplace = ...)` is the
   Laplace prior, and it **defaults to 0** (no smoothing). Separately,
   `predict(..., threshold = 0.001, eps = 0)` replaces zero likelihoods with `threshold`
   at prediction time. So R will not show you a hard zero unless you ask for one.

That third point is a genuine difference from Python worth holding onto:
`sklearn`'s `CategoricalNB` smooths by default (`alpha = 1.0`), so it does *not* reproduce
textbook arithmetic out of the box. `e1071` does not smooth by default, so it *does* — but
it then quietly patches zeros at predict time instead. Neither library is wrong; they just
make opposite defaults, and you have to know which you are using.

# Example 1 — Weather and Golf

Slides 11–13. Fourteen days, one predictor, a binary outcome. The lecture asks: **how
likely are players to play if the weather is sunny?** and answers 0.60.

```{r golf-data}
golf <- data.frame(
  Weather = factor(
    c("Sunny", "Overcast", "Rainy", "Sunny", "Sunny", "Overcast", "Rainy",
      "Rainy", "Sunny", "Rainy", "Sunny", "Overcast", "Overcast", "Rainy"),
    levels = c("Overcast", "Rainy", "Sunny")),
  Play = factor(
    c("No", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "No",
      "No", "Yes", "Yes", "No", "Yes", "Yes", "No"),
    levels = c("No", "Yes"))
)

# Setting levels explicitly is not decoration. It fixes the column order in every table
# below and the encoding e1071 uses internally. Leave it out and you inherit whatever
# alphabetical order happens to produce, which will differ from the slides.
str(golf)
golf
```

## 1.1 The frequency table

`table()` is the counting step from slide 11. Nothing Bayesian has happened yet.

```{r golf-freq}
freq <- table(golf$Weather, golf$Play)
addmargins(freq)          # addmargins() adds the row/column totals
```

This is slide 11 exactly: Overcast 0/4, Rainy 3/2, Sunny 2/3, totals 5 No and 9 Yes.

Note the **0** in Overcast/No. No overcast day was ever a no-play day. That empty cell
comes back in section 1.5.

## 1.2 The likelihood table

Divide by the **column** totals, because we want $P(\text{Weather} \mid \text{Play})$ —
the class is the given, so the class total is the denominator.

`prop.table(x, margin = 2)` normalizes within columns. Getting the margin backwards is
the single most common error here, so check it: each **column** must sum to 1.

```{r golf-lik}
lik <- prop.table(freq, margin = 2)
round(lik, 3)

cat("\ncolumn sums (must be 1):", round(colSums(lik), 3), "\n")
cat("row sums (meaningless -- a row mixes two distributions):",
    round(rowSums(lik), 3), "\n")

prior <- prop.table(table(golf$Play))
cat("\npriors:\n"); print(round(prior, 3))
```

## 1.3 Bayes' theorem by hand

With one predictor the denominator $P(\text{Sunny})$ is just a row total sitting in the
frequency table, so we can apply slide 10 directly:

$$P(\text{Yes} \mid \text{Sunny}) = \frac{P(\text{Sunny} \mid \text{Yes}) \times P(\text{Yes})}{P(\text{Sunny})}$$

```{r golf-hand}
p_sunny_given_yes <- lik["Sunny", "Yes"]                # 3/9
p_sunny_given_no  <- lik["Sunny", "No"]                 # 2/5
p_yes             <- as.numeric(prior["Yes"])           # 9/14
p_no              <- as.numeric(prior["No"])            # 5/14
p_sunny           <- sum(freq["Sunny", ]) / nrow(golf)  # 5/14

post_yes <- p_sunny_given_yes * p_yes / p_sunny
post_no  <- p_sunny_given_no  * p_no  / p_sunny

cat(sprintf("P(Yes | Sunny) = %.4f\n", post_yes))
cat(sprintf("P(No  | Sunny) = %.4f\n", post_no))
cat(sprintf("they sum to      %.4f\n", post_yes + post_no))

# Sanity check straight from the raw data
sunny <- golf[golf$Weather == "Sunny", ]
cat(sprintf("\ndirect count: %d of %d sunny days played = %.4f\n",
            sum(sunny$Play == "Yes"), nrow(sunny),
            mean(sunny$Play == "Yes")))
```

0.60, matching the slide, and the direct count confirms it: 3 of 5 sunny days were
played. With a single predictor Bayes' theorem is *guaranteed* to recover the simple
conditional proportion — it cannot do anything else. Good for checking your
understanding, but it does not yet show what Naive Bayes is for. That is Example 2.

## 1.4 The same thing with `e1071`

No manual encoding step is needed: R factors carry their own levels, so `naiveBayes()`
takes the data frame as-is. (Contrast the Python version, which needs an `OrdinalEncoder`
because `sklearn` only accepts numeric arrays.)

```{r golf-e1071, eval=have_e1071}
# laplace = 0 disables smoothing, matching the lecture's raw-count arithmetic.
# It is already the default; we pass it explicitly so the intent is on the page.
m1 <- naiveBayes(Play ~ Weather, data = golf, laplace = 0)

# newdata must carry the SAME factor levels as the training data. Rebuilding the factor
# with levels = levels(golf$Weather) is the safe idiom; a bare "Sunny" string can be
# matched to the wrong internal code or dropped.
newday <- data.frame(Weather = factor("Sunny", levels = levels(golf$Weather)))

# threshold = 0 switches OFF e1071's predict-time zero patching (see trap 3 above),
# so what we get back is the unmodified textbook computation.
pred_raw <- predict(m1, newdata = newday, type = "raw", threshold = 0, eps = 0)

cat("e1071:\n"); print(round(pred_raw, 4))
cat(sprintf("\nby hand:  No %.4f   Yes %.4f\n", post_no, post_yes))
cat("\npredicted class:",
    as.character(predict(m1, newdata = newday, type = "class")), "\n")
```

Now open the fitted object and confirm the numbers inside it are the two tables we built
by hand.

```{r golf-inside, eval=have_e1071}
cat("--- m1$apriori : the class counts (not yet proportions) ---\n")
print(m1$apriori)
cat("\nas proportions:\n")
print(round(prop.table(m1$apriori), 3))

cat("\n--- m1$tables$Weather : the likelihoods ---\n")
print(round(m1$tables$Weather, 3))

cat("\n--- what we built with prop.table() ---\n")
print(round(t(lik), 3))
```

Two things to notice.

`m1$apriori` holds **counts**, not probabilities — wrap it in `prop.table()` to compare
with our priors. And `m1$tables$Weather` is the **transpose** of our `lik`: `e1071` puts
classes in rows and feature levels in columns. That is why `t(lik)` is needed to line
them up. Neither convention is wrong, but mixing them up produces a table that looks
plausible and is silently wrong, so always check which way round you are.

The model *is* those tables. Training a Naive Bayes classifier is counting and dividing —
no optimizer, no iteration. That is why it costs nothing to use as a baseline.

## 1.5 The empty cell, and R's hidden third smoothing

`P(Overcast | No) = 0`. Watch what happens with zero patching off, then on.

```{r golf-zero, eval=have_e1071}
overcast <- data.frame(Weather = factor("Overcast", levels = levels(golf$Weather)))

cat("threshold = 0  (patching OFF -- the true unsmoothed result):\n")
print(round(predict(m1, overcast, type = "raw", threshold = 0, eps = 0), 4))
cat("-> 100% certainty from one empty cell in 14 rows.\n")

cat("\nthreshold = 0.001 (e1071's DEFAULT -- zeros quietly replaced):\n")
print(round(predict(m1, overcast, type = "raw"), 4))

cat("\nlaplace = 1 (proper add-one smoothing at fit time):\n")
m1_smooth <- naiveBayes(Play ~ Weather, data = golf, laplace = 1)
print(round(predict(m1_smooth, overcast, type = "raw", threshold = 0), 4))
cat("\nP(Yes | Sunny) under laplace = 1:\n")
print(round(predict(m1_smooth, newday, type = "raw", threshold = 0), 4))
```

Three different answers for the same question, from one library, depending on arguments
most people never pass. Worth dwelling on:

- `threshold = 0` gives the honest unsmoothed answer: a degenerate 0/1.
- The **default** `threshold = 0.001` hides the degeneracy by substituting an arbitrary
  small number. It is a patch, not a principled prior, and the value 0.001 has no
  justification beyond being small.
- `laplace = 1` is the actual fix from the lecture. It changes the *fitted model*, spreads
  probability mass according to a stated prior, and its influence shrinks as $n$ grows.

Prefer `laplace`. And when reporting results, say which you used.

# Example 2 — Predicting Voter Turnout

Fourteen respondents, three predictors, one binary outcome.

| Variable | Values | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `Age` | Young / Middle / Senior | predictor |
| `Contacted` | Yes / No — reached by a canvasser? | predictor |
| `Interest` | High / Low — interest in politics | predictor |
| `Vote` | **Yes / No** | class to predict |

Three predictors is what makes this worth doing. The joint
$P(\text{Age}, \text{Contacted}, \text{Interest} \mid c)$ cannot be estimated from 14
rows — almost every three-way combination appears zero or one time — so we need the
independence assumption that gives the method its name.

```{r voter-data}
voters <- data.frame(
  Age = c("Young", "Young", "Middle", "Senior", "Senior", "Senior", "Middle",
          "Young", "Young", "Senior", "Young", "Middle", "Middle", "Senior"),
  Contacted = c("No", "No", "No", "No", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes",
                "No", "Yes", "No", "Yes", "Yes", "No", "No"),
  Interest = c("Low", "High", "High", "Low", "High", "High", "High",
               "Low", "Low", "High", "Low", "Low", "High", "Low"),
  Vote = c("No", "No", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "No", "Yes",
           "No", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "No")
)

# Trap 1 in action: after this data.frame() call, all four columns are CHARACTER, not
# factor (R >= 4.0). Convert explicitly, with the level order we want.
voters$Age       <- factor(voters$Age,       levels = c("Young", "Middle", "Senior"))
voters$Contacted <- factor(voters$Contacted, levels = c("No", "Yes"))
voters$Interest  <- factor(voters$Interest,  levels = c("Low", "High"))
voters$Vote      <- factor(voters$Vote,      levels = c("No", "Yes"))

FEATURES <- c("Age", "Contacted", "Interest")

stopifnot(all(sapply(voters, is.factor)))   # fail loudly rather than model silently
table(voters$Vote)
voters
```

## 2.1 One frequency table per predictor

This is the structural consequence of the independence assumption: three small marginal
tables instead of one 12-cell joint table that 14 observations could never fill.

```{r voter-freq}
for (f in FEATURES) {
  cat("---", f, "---\n")
  print(addmargins(table(voters[[f]], voters$Vote)))
  cat("\n")
}
```

Every table has the same column totals (5 No, 9 Yes) and sums to 14. If yours doesn't,
you miscounted.

`Middle`/`No` is **0** — no middle-aged respondent failed to vote. Section 2.4.

## 2.2 Naive Bayes written out longhand

Before reaching for a package, here is the whole algorithm in twenty lines of base R.
Nothing is hidden, so this is the ground truth against which everything else is checked.

```{r nb-by-hand}
nb_by_hand <- function(data, features, values, target = "Vote",
                       laplace = 0, verbose = TRUE) {
  # Score every class for one observation. Returns normalized posteriors.
  # laplace > 0 adds that many pseudo-counts to each category of each feature.
  n      <- nrow(data)
  labels <- levels(data[[target]])
  scores <- setNames(numeric(length(labels)), labels)

  for (lab in labels) {
    sub   <- data[data[[target]] == lab, , drop = FALSE]
    n_c   <- nrow(sub)
    score <- n_c / n                                   # the prior P(c)
    parts <- sprintf("P(%s)=%.3f", lab, score)

    for (k in seq_along(features)) {
      f <- features[k]
      v <- values[k]
      k_levels <- nlevels(data[[f]])                   # k, for the smoothing denominator
      lk <- (sum(sub[[f]] == v) + laplace) / (n_c + laplace * k_levels)
      score <- score * lk
      parts <- c(parts, sprintf("P(%s=%s|%s)=%.3f", f, v, lab, lk))
    }

    scores[lab] <- score
    if (verbose) cat("  ", paste(parts, collapse = " x "),
                     sprintf(" = %.6f\n", score))
  }

  total <- sum(scores)
  if (total == 0) {
    if (verbose) cat("  every class scored exactly 0 -- undefined\n")
    return(scores * NaN)
  }
  scores / total
}

new_case <- c("Senior", "Yes", "High")
cat("Scoring Age=Senior, Contacted=Yes, Interest=High\n")
post2 <- nb_by_hand(voters, FEATURES, new_case)
cat("\nposteriors:\n"); print(round(post2, 4))
```

About 0.853 for Yes and 0.147 for No — the numbers from the slides. This person is
predicted to vote, with roughly 85% confidence.

## 2.3 The same thing with `e1071`

```{r voter-e1071, eval=have_e1071}
m2 <- naiveBayes(Vote ~ Age + Contacted + Interest, data = voters, laplace = 0)

# Build newdata with matching levels for every column. Doing this with a small helper
# is worth the trouble -- mismatched levels are the most common source of silently
# wrong predictions in R.
make_row <- function(values, template, features) {
  row <- lapply(seq_along(features), function(k)
    factor(values[k], levels = levels(template[[features[k]]])))
  names(row) <- features
  as.data.frame(row, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}

q2 <- make_row(new_case, voters, FEATURES)
print(q2)

cat("\ne1071:\n")
print(round(predict(m2, q2, type = "raw", threshold = 0, eps = 0), 4))
cat("\nby hand:\n"); print(round(post2, 4))
```

## 2.4 Which predictor drove the prediction?

Naive Bayes decomposes into one factor per predictor, so you can always say which feature
did the work. The ratio of the two likelihoods tells you which way a term pushes: above 1
favours Yes, below 1 favours No.

```{r voter-contrib, eval=have_e1071}
contribution_table <- function(model, values, features) {
  pri <- prop.table(model$apriori)
  rows <- list(data.frame(term = "prior",
                          No = as.numeric(pri["No"]),
                          Yes = as.numeric(pri["Yes"])))
  for (k in seq_along(features)) {
    tab <- model$tables[[features[k]]]     # rows = class, cols = level
    rows[[k + 1]] <- data.frame(
      term = paste0(features[k], " = ", values[k]),
      No   = tab["No",  values[k]],
      Yes  = tab["Yes", values[k]])
  }
  out <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  out$ratio_Yes_No <- out$Yes / out$No
  out
}

contrib <- contribution_table(m2, new_case, FEATURES)
print(format(contrib, digits = 3))
cat(sprintf("\nproduct of the ratios = %.3f  <- the odds in favour of Yes\n",
            prod(contrib$ratio_Yes_No)))
```

Read the ratio column: being contacted is the strongest signal (roughly 2.8 to 1 toward
voting), high interest helps mildly, and being Senior leans *slightly against* voting
(ratio below 1) but is outweighed. Multiply the ratios and you get the final odds — the
same computation rearranged.

## 2.5 The zero-frequency problem

Now classify someone **Middle** aged, **not contacted**, **Low** interest.
$P(\text{Middle} \mid \text{No}) = 0$, and one zero annihilates the whole product.

```{r voter-zero}
hard_case <- c("Middle", "No", "Low")
cat("Age=Middle, Contacted=No, Interest=Low  (laplace = 0)\n")
post_hard <- nb_by_hand(voters, FEATURES, hard_case)
cat("\nposteriors:\n"); print(round(post_hard, 4))
cat("\nThe other two predictors both lean 'No', and the zero wiped them out\n",
    "before they could contribute.\n")
```

```{r voter-zero-e1071, eval=have_e1071}
q_hard <- make_row(hard_case, voters, FEATURES)

cat("e1071, threshold = 0 (honest):        ")
cat(round(predict(m2, q_hard, type = "raw", threshold = 0, eps = 0), 4), "\n")
cat("e1071, default threshold = 0.001:     ")
cat(round(predict(m2, q_hard, type = "raw"), 4), "\n")
cat("   ^ the default hides the collapse instead of fixing it\n")
```

## 2.6 Laplace smoothing, the actual fix

$$P(x_i \mid c) = \frac{\text{count} + \alpha}{n_c + \alpha k}$$

where $k$ is the number of categories that predictor has.

```{r voter-laplace}
cat("laplace = 1, by hand:\n")
post_smooth <- nb_by_hand(voters, FEATURES, hard_case, laplace = 1)
cat("\nposteriors:\n"); print(round(post_smooth, 4))
cat("-> 0.248 / 0.752, matching the smoothed arithmetic from the slides\n")
```

```{r voter-laplace-e1071, eval=have_e1071}
m2_smooth <- naiveBayes(Vote ~ Age + Contacted + Interest, data = voters, laplace = 1)
cat("e1071 with laplace = 1:\n")
print(round(predict(m2_smooth, q_hard, type = "raw", threshold = 0), 4))

cat("\nWhat smoothing did to the Age likelihoods:\n")
comparison <- rbind(
  `laplace=0` = m2$tables$Age["No", ],
  `laplace=1` = m2_smooth$tables$Age["No", ])
cat("\nP(Age | Vote = No):\n"); print(round(comparison, 3))
cat("\nNote: the empty Middle cell moves 0.000 -> 0.125, while the well-supported\n",
    "cells barely move. That asymmetry is exactly what you want.\n")
```

### How much does $\alpha$ matter?

```{r voter-alpha-sweep}
alphas <- c(0, 0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 20)

sweep <- data.frame(
  alpha = alphas,
  P_Yes_SeniorYesHigh = sapply(alphas, function(a)
    nb_by_hand(voters, FEATURES, new_case,  laplace = a, verbose = FALSE)[["Yes"]]),
  P_Yes_MiddleNoLow = sapply(alphas, function(a)
    nb_by_hand(voters, FEATURES, hard_case, laplace = a, verbose = FALSE)[["Yes"]])
)
print(round(sweep, 4))
```

```{r voter-alpha-plot, fig.height=4}
# A log x-axis cannot show alpha = 0, so plot the positive values and note the
# alpha = 0 endpoint separately (it is in the table above).
sw <- sweep[sweep$alpha > 0, ]

plot(sw$alpha, sw$P_Yes_MiddleNoLow, type = "b", pch = 19, log = "x",
     ylim = c(0.5, 1.05), col = "#b03030",
     xlab = expression(alpha ~ "(log scale; " * alpha == 0 * " omitted)"),
     ylab = "P(Vote = Yes | x)",
     main = "Smoothing drags both predictions toward the base rate")
lines(sw$alpha, sw$P_Yes_SeniorYesHigh, type = "b", pch = 17, col = "#20607a")
abline(h = mean(voters$Vote == "Yes"), lty = 2, col = "grey40")
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.85,
       legend = c("Middle / No / Low (had the zero)",
                  "Senior / Yes / High",
                  "base rate 9/14"),
       col = c("#b03030", "#20607a", "grey40"),
       pch = c(19, 17, NA), lty = c(1, 1, 2))
```

As $\alpha$ grows every estimate is dragged toward uniform and both predictions decay
toward the base rate. With 14 rows, $\alpha = 20$ has essentially erased the data. The
effect shrinks as $n$ grows, which is why the same value is decisive here and harmless on
the 32,000-row dataset in Example 3.

## 2.7 An honest caveat

Rows 5 and 6 have **identical predictors and opposite outcomes**.

```{r voter-dup}
dup <- voters[voters$Age == "Senior" & voters$Contacted == "Yes" &
              voters$Interest == "High", ]
print(dup)
cat(sprintf("\nActual outcome for this exact profile: %d of %d voted. Model said 0.85.\n",
            sum(dup$Vote == "Yes"), nrow(dup)))
```

So the truthful answer for that profile is 50/50, and our 85% is overconfident. That gap
is the independence assumption showing its cost: multiplying three separately favourable
likelihoods treats them as three independent witnesses when they overlap (canvassers
plausibly target older or more engaged voters). Evidence gets double-counted and the
posterior is pushed too far from 0.5.

This is the standard, well-documented weakness: Naive Bayes **rankings and hard decisions
are often fine, its probabilities are not**. We measure that directly in Example 3.

---

# Example 3 — Income, Education and Inequality (1994 US Census)

## The dataset

The **UCI "Adult" / Census Income** data is an extract from the 1994 US Census Current
Population Survey, assembled by Barry Becker and Ronny Kohavi. UCI files it under
*Social Science*, and it has been central to both machine learning and
algorithmic-fairness research for thirty years.

- Source: <https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/2/adult>
- Citation: Becker, B. & Kohavi, R. (1996). *Adult*. UCI Machine Learning Repository.
  <https://doi.org/10.24432/C5XW20> (CC BY 4.0)

**Task:** predict whether annual income exceeds \$50,000 from education, occupation,
marital status, hours worked, sex, race, age and so on.

We load `adult.data`, the 32,561-row training portion. (A further 16,281 rows live in
`adult.test`, which uses a slightly different label format — `>50K.` with a trailing
period. Combining them is exercise 5.)

## Why this is a sociology problem

The features are exactly the variables stratification research cares about. Fitting a
classifier here asks *how legible is the income distribution from demographic
characteristics alone?* — and, more interestingly, *which characteristics carry the most
information, and for whom does the model fail?*

Three things to keep in view:

1. **The \$50,000 threshold is arbitrary and dated.** In 1994 dollars it sat near the
   80th percentile of individual earnings. Dichotomising a continuous outcome discards
   information, and where you cut determines what "high income" means.
2. **Prediction is not explanation.** A large weight on `marital-status` does not mean
   marriage causes income.
3. **The independence assumption will be badly violated**, in ways we can measure
   (section 3.8).

## 3.1 Loading the data

```{r adult-load, cache=TRUE}
COLUMNS <- c("age", "workclass", "fnlwgt", "education", "education_num",
             "marital_status", "occupation", "relationship", "race", "sex",
             "capital_gain", "capital_loss", "hours_per_week",
             "native_country", "income")

UCI_URL <- paste0("https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/machine-learning-databases/",
                  "adult/adult.data")
LOCAL <- "adult.csv"

load_adult <- function() {
  if (file.exists(LOCAL)) {
    cat("loading cached", LOCAL, "\n")
    return(read.csv(LOCAL, stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
  }
  cat("downloading from the UCI archive ...\n")
  df <- read.csv(UCI_URL,
                 header = FALSE,
                 col.names = COLUMNS,
                 strip.white = TRUE,     # UCI pads fields with leading spaces
                 na.strings = c("?", ""), # UCI codes missing as a literal "?"
                 stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  write.csv(df, LOCAL, row.names = FALSE)
  cat("cached to", LOCAL, "\n")
  df
}

adult <- load_adult()

# Trailing periods appear in adult.test; harmless to strip here too.
adult$income <- sub("\\.$", "", trimws(adult$income))

cat(sprintf("%s rows x %d columns\n", format(nrow(adult), big.mark = ","), ncol(adult)))
str(adult, vec.len = 2)
```

## 3.2 What are we looking at?

Always do this first: how imbalanced is the outcome, where are the missing values, does
anything look wrong?

```{r adult-explore}
cat("--- outcome ---\n")
print(table(adult$income))
base_rate <- mean(adult$income == ">50K")
cat(sprintf("\nbase rate: %.4f earn >50K\n", base_rate))
cat(sprintf("-> always guessing '<=50K' is %.1f%% accurate and has learned nothing.\n",
            100 * (1 - base_rate)))
cat("   Accuracy will be a poor summary of this model.\n")

cat("\n--- missing values ---\n")
miss <- colSums(is.na(adult))
print(miss[miss > 0])

cat("\n--- numeric summary ---\n")
print(summary(adult[, c("age", "hours_per_week", "capital_gain",
                        "capital_loss", "education_num", "fnlwgt")]))

cat("\n--- distinct values per character column ---\n")
chr_cols <- names(adult)[sapply(adult, is.character)]
print(sort(sapply(adult[chr_cols], function(x) length(unique(x))), decreasing = TRUE))
```

Two columns need a decision, and both decisions are substantive rather than technical:

- **`fnlwgt`** is the census *sampling weight* — how many people in the population each
  row represents. It is not a property of the person and must not be a predictor. (It
  arguably should be used to weight the analysis, which is a real limitation of how this
  dataset is almost always modelled, including here.)
- **`education_num`** is a numeric recoding of `education`. Including both feeds the same
  information in twice, and because Naive Bayes multiplies likelihoods, duplicated
  evidence gets counted twice over. We keep the readable categorical version.

## 3.3 Feature engineering

We put everything through the categorical path, which means binning the continuous
variables. A real trade-off:

- **Cost:** binning discards within-bin variation and the cut points are our invention.
- **Benefit:** it drops the normality assumption `naiveBayes()` would otherwise impose on
  numeric columns. For `age` that assumption is defensible; for `capital_gain` it is not —
  it is zero for about 92% of people and enormous for a few. No normal distribution fits
  that, and letting `e1071` fit one anyway would corrupt every prediction involving it.

So `capital_gain` and `capital_loss` become yes/no indicators, which is closer to what
they measure: whether someone holds income-generating assets.

```{r adult-features}
d <- adult

d$age_band <- cut(d$age,
                  breaks = c(16, 24, 34, 44, 54, 64, Inf),
                  labels = c("17-24", "25-34", "35-44", "45-54", "55-64", "65+"))

d$hours_band <- cut(d$hours_per_week,
                    breaks = c(0, 34, 44, 59, Inf),
                    labels = c("part-time (<35)", "full-time (35-44)",
                               "long (45-59)", "very long (60+)"))

d$capital_gain_yn <- ifelse(d$capital_gain > 0, "yes", "no")
d$capital_loss_yn <- ifelse(d$capital_loss > 0, "yes", "no")

CAT <- c("age_band", "hours_band", "capital_gain_yn", "capital_loss_yn",
         "workclass", "education", "marital_status", "occupation",
         "relationship", "race", "sex", "native_country")

cat(sprintf("share with any capital gain: %.4f\n", mean(d$capital_gain > 0)))
cat(sprintf("share with any capital loss: %.4f\n", mean(d$capital_loss > 0)))
cat("\nage bands:\n");   print(table(d$age_band))
cat("\nhours bands:\n"); print(table(d$hours_band))
```

### Missing values become their own category

Rather than drop rows, make `"Missing"` a level. For a categorical Naive Bayes this is
cheap and often better than imputation: if non-response is itself informative (and in
labour-force surveys it usually is) the model can learn from it. Dropping the rows throws
that away and biases the sample.

### Then convert everything to factors — deliberately, not by accident

This is trap 1. `read.csv()` gave us character columns. `naiveBayes()` needs factors to
treat a column as categorical. We convert explicitly and then *assert* it.

```{r adult-factors}
for (v in CAT) {
  x <- as.character(d[[v]])
  x[is.na(x)] <- "Missing"
  d[[v]] <- factor(x)
}

d$income <- factor(d$income, levels = c("<=50K", ">50K"))

# Fail loudly rather than fit a Gaussian by mistake.
stopifnot(all(sapply(d[CAT], is.factor)), is.factor(d$income))

cat("levels per feature:\n")
print(sapply(d[CAT], nlevels))

cat("\n'Missing' now appears where relevant:\n")
for (v in c("workclass", "occupation", "native_country")) {
  n <- sum(d[[v]] == "Missing")
  cat(sprintf("  %-16s %5d rows (%.2f%%)\n", v, n, 100 * n / nrow(d)))
}
```

### Collapsing ultra-rare levels

One more step, and it is not cosmetic. `native_country` has 42 levels, several with a
handful of observations (`Holand-Netherlands` has exactly **one** row in the whole
dataset). Two problems follow:

- **Statistically**, a likelihood estimated from one observation is noise. Laplace
  smoothing keeps it from being zero but cannot make it informative.
- **Mechanically**, a level with one row may land entirely in the test split, and then
  `glm()` fails outright with *"factor has new levels"* when we try to predict. Naive
  Bayes tolerates this; logistic regression does not.

So we merge levels below a minimum count into `"Other"` before splitting. Note this is
outcome-independent — we are counting rows, not looking at income — so it is safe to do on
the full dataset.

```{r adult-lump}
lump_rare <- function(f, min_count = 20, other = "Other") {
  tab  <- table(f)
  rare <- names(tab)[tab < min_count]
  if (!length(rare)) return(droplevels(f))
  levels(f)[levels(f) %in% rare] <- other
  droplevels(f)
}

levels_before <- sapply(d[CAT], nlevels)
for (v in CAT) d[[v]] <- lump_rare(d[[v]], min_count = 20)
levels_after <- sapply(d[CAT], nlevels)

changed <- data.frame(feature = CAT,
                      before = as.integer(levels_before),
                      after  = as.integer(levels_after))
changed <- changed[changed$before != changed$after, ]
if (nrow(changed)) {
  cat("features whose level count shrank:\n")
  print(changed, row.names = FALSE)
} else {
  cat("no levels were rare enough to merge\n")
}

cat(sprintf("\nsmallest level count remaining: %d\n",
            min(sapply(d[CAT], function(f) min(table(f))))))
```

## 3.4 Train/test split, stratified

`sample()` on its own gives an unstratified split, which with imbalanced data can hand
you a test set with a noticeably different base rate. We stratify by splitting within
each class.

```{r adult-split}
set.seed(42)

stratified_split <- function(y, test_frac = 0.25) {
  test_idx <- unlist(lapply(levels(y), function(lev) {
    idx <- which(y == lev)
    sample(idx, size = round(test_frac * length(idx)))
  }))
  sort(test_idx)
}

test_idx  <- stratified_split(d$income, 0.25)
train_idx <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(d)), test_idx)

train <- d[train_idx, ]
test  <- d[test_idx, ]

cat(sprintf("train %s   test %s\n",
            format(nrow(train), big.mark = ","),
            format(nrow(test),  big.mark = ",")))
cat(sprintf("base rate  train %.4f   test %.4f\n",
            mean(train$income == ">50K"), mean(test$income == ">50K")))
```

## 3.5 Metric helpers

No `caret` or `pROC` dependency. AUC comes from the rank-based Mann-Whitney identity,
which is exact and handles ties by average ranks:

$$\text{AUC} = \frac{\sum_{i \in \text{pos}} r_i - n_{\text{pos}}(n_{\text{pos}} + 1)/2}{n_{\text{pos}} \, n_{\text{neg}}}$$

```{r adult-metrics}
auc_score <- function(labels, scores) {
  # labels: 0/1 numeric. scores: higher = more likely positive.
  pos <- scores[labels == 1]
  neg <- scores[labels == 0]
  if (!length(pos) || !length(neg)) return(NA_real_)
  r <- rank(c(pos, neg))                       # average ranks for ties
  (sum(r[seq_along(pos)]) - length(pos) * (length(pos) + 1) / 2) /
    (length(pos) * length(neg))
}

classification_report <- function(truth, pred, positive = ">50K") {
  cm <- table(actual = truth, predicted = pred)
  tp <- sum(truth == positive  & pred == positive)
  fp <- sum(truth != positive  & pred == positive)
  fn <- sum(truth == positive  & pred != positive)
  tn <- sum(truth != positive  & pred != positive)
  prec <- if ((tp + fp) > 0) tp / (tp + fp) else NA_real_
  rec  <- if ((tp + fn) > 0) tp / (tp + fn) else NA_real_
  spec <- if ((tn + fp) > 0) tn / (tn + fp) else NA_real_
  list(
    confusion = cm,
    accuracy = (tp + tn) / length(truth),
    balanced_accuracy = mean(c(rec, spec)),
    precision = prec,
    recall = rec,
    f1 = if (!is.na(prec) && !is.na(rec) && (prec + rec) > 0)
           2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec) else NA_real_
  )
}

# quick self-test on a case we can verify by inspection
stopifnot(abs(auc_score(c(0, 0, 1, 1), c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4)) - 1) < 1e-9)
stopifnot(abs(auc_score(c(0, 1), c(0.5, 0.5)) - 0.5) < 1e-9)  # a tie is worth 0.5
cat("metric helpers self-tested OK\n")
```

## 3.6 Fit, and compare against honest baselines

A model's accuracy means nothing alone. Two reference points:

- **Majority-class baseline** — the floor. About 76% accurate here, having learned nothing.
- **Logistic regression** (`glm`) — comparable simplicity, but does *not* assume feature
  independence. If Naive Bayes lands far below it, the independence assumption is costing
  us; if close, it is doing little harm.

```{r adult-fit, eval=have_e1071}
form <- as.formula(paste("income ~", paste(CAT, collapse = " + ")))

m3 <- naiveBayes(form, data = train, laplace = 1)

# We leave predict()'s threshold at its default here. With laplace = 1 there are no
# zero likelihoods left for it to patch, so it never fires -- unlike Examples 1 and 2,
# where we had to switch it off to see the honest result.
prob_nb <- predict(m3, test, type = "raw")[, ">50K"]
pred_nb <- predict(m3, test, type = "class")

y_test_num <- as.integer(test$income == ">50K")

rep_nb <- classification_report(test$income, pred_nb)

# --- majority baseline ---
majority <- factor(rep("<=50K", nrow(test)), levels = levels(test$income))
rep_maj  <- classification_report(test$income, majority)

# --- logistic regression ---
# Guard against the failure mode described in 3.3: any factor level present in test but
# absent from train makes predict.glm() error out. After lumping this should never fire,
# but check rather than trust.
unseen <- unlist(lapply(CAT, function(v) {
  miss <- setdiff(levels(droplevels(test[[v]])), levels(droplevels(train[[v]])))
  if (length(miss)) paste0(v, ": ", paste(miss, collapse = ", ")) else NULL
}))
if (length(unseen)) {
  cat("WARNING -- levels in test but not train:\n"); cat(unseen, sep = "\n")
} else {
  cat("level check passed: every test level appears in train\n")
}

glm_fit <- glm(form, data = train, family = binomial())
prob_lr <- predict(glm_fit, newdata = test, type = "response")
pred_lr <- factor(ifelse(prob_lr > 0.5, ">50K", "<=50K"),
                  levels = levels(test$income))
rep_lr  <- classification_report(test$income, pred_lr)

results <- data.frame(
  model = c("majority baseline", "naiveBayes (laplace=1)", "logistic regression"),
  accuracy = c(rep_maj$accuracy, rep_nb$accuracy, rep_lr$accuracy),
  balanced_acc = c(rep_maj$balanced_accuracy, rep_nb$balanced_accuracy,
                   rep_lr$balanced_accuracy),
  AUC = c(NA, auc_score(y_test_num, prob_nb), auc_score(y_test_num, prob_lr))
)
print(format(results, digits = 4))
```

**Reading that table.** Look at `balanced_acc` and `AUC`, not `accuracy`. The majority
baseline posts a high accuracy and a balanced accuracy of exactly 0.50 — it is right
about everyone who earns less and wrong about everyone who earns more. Balanced accuracy
averages the per-class recall, so it exposes that at once. AUC asks a different and often
more useful question: draw one high earner and one low earner at random; how often does
the model score the high earner higher?

```{r adult-cm, eval=have_e1071}
cat("--- confusion matrix, naiveBayes ---\n")
print(rep_nb$confusion)
cat(sprintf("\naccuracy          %.4f\nbalanced accuracy %.4f\n",
            rep_nb$accuracy, rep_nb$balanced_accuracy))
cat(sprintf("precision (>50K)  %.4f\nrecall    (>50K)  %.4f\nF1        (>50K)  %.4f\n",
            rep_nb$precision, rep_nb$recall, rep_nb$f1))
```

Mind the gap between precision and recall on `>50K`. Which matters depends entirely on
the application, and that is a substantive question. If this model screened people for a
benefits programme, a false negative (missing someone who needs help) and a false positive
(enrolling someone who does not) carry very different human costs, and no single number
captures the trade-off.

```{r adult-roc, eval=have_e1071}
roc_points <- function(labels, scores) {
  o <- order(scores, decreasing = TRUE)
  lab <- labels[o]
  tpr <- cumsum(lab == 1) / sum(lab == 1)
  fpr <- cumsum(lab == 0) / sum(lab == 0)
  data.frame(fpr = c(0, fpr), tpr = c(0, tpr))
}

r_nb <- roc_points(y_test_num, prob_nb)
r_lr <- roc_points(y_test_num, prob_lr)

plot(r_nb$fpr, r_nb$tpr, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#20607a",
     xlab = "false positive rate", ylab = "true positive rate",
     main = "Predicting income > $50K, 1994 US Census")
lines(r_lr$fpr, r_lr$tpr, lwd = 2, col = "#b03030")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
legend("bottomright", bty = "n",
       legend = c(sprintf("naiveBayes (AUC %.3f)", auc_score(y_test_num, prob_nb)),
                  sprintf("logistic regression (AUC %.3f)", auc_score(y_test_num, prob_lr)),
                  "chance"),
       col = c("#20607a", "#b03030", "grey50"), lwd = c(2, 2, 1), lty = c(1, 1, 2))
```

## 3.7 Interpretation: which characteristics carry information?

The part a sociologist actually wants. For each category compute the **evidence weight**

$$w = \log \frac{P(\text{category} \mid >\$50\text{K})}{P(\text{category} \mid \le\$50\text{K})}$$

Positive means the category is more common among high earners, so observing it shifts the
prediction upward. This reads straight off `m3$tables` — no extra fitting, because the
trained model already *is* these tables.

Two warnings before reading the output. These are **associations in 1994 survey data**,
not causal effects and not current facts. And a weight can be large while the category is
rare, so always read the probabilities beside the ratio.

```{r adult-evidence, eval=have_e1071}
evidence_weights <- function(model, feature, min_share = 0.01) {
  tab <- model$tables[[feature]]          # rows = class, cols = level
  out <- data.frame(
    category      = colnames(tab),
    p_given_low   = as.numeric(tab["<=50K", ]),
    p_given_high  = as.numeric(tab[">50K",  ]),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  out$evidence_weight <- log(out$p_given_high / out$p_given_low)
  out <- out[pmax(out$p_given_low, out$p_given_high) >= min_share, ]
  out[order(-out$evidence_weight), ]
}

for (f in c("education", "marital_status", "occupation")) {
  cat("\n===", f, strrep("=", max(0, 46 - nchar(f))), "\n")
  print(format(evidence_weights(m3, f), digits = 3), row.names = FALSE)
}
```

```{r adult-evidence-plot, eval=have_e1071, fig.height=9, fig.width=8}
op <- par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(4, 11, 3, 1))
for (f in c("education", "marital_status", "occupation")) {
  ew <- evidence_weights(m3, f)
  ew <- ew[order(ew$evidence_weight), ]
  barplot(ew$evidence_weight, names.arg = ew$category, horiz = TRUE, las = 1,
          col = ifelse(ew$evidence_weight < 0, "#b03030", "#20607a"),
          cex.names = 0.75, xlab = "log P(cat | >50K) / P(cat | <=50K)",
          main = f)
  abline(v = 0, lwd = 1)
}
par(op)
```

### What to look for, and how to be careful

Read the education panel first. The ordering should be close to monotone in credential
level, which is the most robust finding in stratification research and a good sign the
model is picking up something real rather than noise.

Then read `marital_status`, carefully. `Married-civ-spouse` will almost certainly carry a
large positive weight, and it is tempting to narrate that as "marriage raises income." At
least four mechanisms are tangled in that one number, and this model separates none of
them:

1. **Selection** — higher earners are more likely to marry in the first place.
2. **Measurement** — the income variable interacts with household and filing structure.
3. **Age confounding** — married people are older, and earnings rise with age.
4. **Gendered specialisation** within households.

A Naive Bayes weight is a *marginal* association: it compares married to unmarried people
without holding age, education or occupation constant. This is precisely where a
classifier stops being able to answer the question you want answered and you need a
research design instead.

## 3.8 Auditing the independence assumption

We assumed the predictors are conditionally independent given income. Let's measure how
false that is with **Cramér's V**, a chi-squared-based association measure for two
categorical variables scaled to $[0, 1]$.

```{r adult-cramer}
cramers_v <- function(a, b) {
  tab <- table(a, b)
  if (any(dim(tab) < 2)) return(NA_real_)
  chi2 <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab, correct = FALSE)$statistic)
  n <- sum(tab)
  as.numeric(sqrt((chi2 / n) / max(1, min(dim(tab) - 1))))
}

V <- outer(seq_along(CAT), seq_along(CAT), Vectorize(function(i, j) {
  if (i == j) 1 else cramers_v(d[[CAT[i]]], d[[CAT[j]]])
}))
dimnames(V) <- list(CAT, CAT)

# strongest pairs, upper triangle only
ut <- which(upper.tri(V), arr.ind = TRUE)
pairs_df <- data.frame(
  a = CAT[ut[, 1]], b = CAT[ut[, 2]], V = V[ut]
)
pairs_df <- pairs_df[order(-pairs_df$V), ]
cat("most strongly associated predictor pairs:\n")
print(format(head(pairs_df, 10), digits = 3), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r adult-cramer-plot, fig.height=6.5, fig.width=7.5}
op <- par(mar = c(9, 9, 3, 2))
# z[i, k] must be V[i, p + 1 - k] so that the y axis reads top-to-bottom
image(seq_along(CAT), seq_along(CAT), V[, rev(seq_along(CAT))],
      col = hcl.colors(24, "YlOrRd", rev = TRUE), zlim = c(0, 1),
      axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
      main = "Cramer's V between predictors\n(Naive Bayes assumes every off-diagonal cell is 0)")
axis(1, at = seq_along(CAT), labels = CAT, las = 2, cex.axis = 0.7)
axis(2, at = seq_along(CAT), labels = rev(CAT), las = 1, cex.axis = 0.7)
box()
par(op)
```

Naive Bayes assumes every off-diagonal cell there is zero. It is not. The
`marital_status` / `relationship` / `sex` cluster should stand out sharply —
`relationship` takes values like `Husband` and `Wife`, which encode marital status and sex
*by construction*, so the model counts the same fact up to three times.

Yet the AUC above was respectable. That is the enduring puzzle about Naive Bayes, and the
resolution is worth stating precisely: violated independence corrupts the *probabilities*
far more than the *ranking*. Double-counted evidence pushes posteriors toward 0 and 1, but
it usually pushes them in the direction they were already going, so the ordering of cases
— and hence AUC, and hence the argmax decision — survives.

### Does dropping the redundancy help?

```{r adult-trim, eval=have_e1071}
CAT_TRIM <- setdiff(CAT, "relationship")
form_trim <- as.formula(paste("income ~", paste(CAT_TRIM, collapse = " + ")))

m3_trim <- naiveBayes(form_trim, data = train, laplace = 1)
prob_trim <- predict(m3_trim, test, type = "raw")[, ">50K"]

cat(sprintf("with 'relationship':    AUC %.4f\n", auc_score(y_test_num, prob_nb)))
cat(sprintf("without 'relationship': AUC %.4f\n", auc_score(y_test_num, prob_trim)))
cat("\nIf dropping a redundant feature barely moves AUC while that feature had a high\n",
    "Cramer's V with others, you are seeing the effect described above: the ranking was\n",
    "robust to the violation even though the probabilities were not.\n")
```

## 3.9 Calibration: are the probabilities trustworthy?

In Example 2 we predicted 0.85 for a profile whose true rate was 0.50. Let's measure that
failure mode properly. Group the test set by predicted probability and compare the average
prediction in each bucket to the actual rate. A calibrated model puts those close together.

```{r adult-calib, eval=have_e1071}
calibration_table <- function(p, y, n_bins = 10) {
  bucket <- cut(p, breaks = seq(0, 1, length.out = n_bins + 1),
                include.lowest = TRUE)
  groups <- split(data.frame(p = p, y = y), bucket, drop = TRUE)
  out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(groups), function(nm) {
    g <- groups[[nm]]
    data.frame(bucket = nm, n = nrow(g),
               mean_predicted = mean(g$p), actual_rate = mean(g$y))
  }))
  out$gap <- out$mean_predicted - out$actual_rate
  out
}

cal_nb <- calibration_table(prob_nb, y_test_num)
print(format(cal_nb, digits = 3), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r adult-calib-plot, eval=have_e1071, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.8}
cal_lr <- calibration_table(prob_lr, y_test_num)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))

plot(cal_nb$mean_predicted, cal_nb$actual_rate, type = "b", pch = 19, lwd = 2,
     col = "#20607a", xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "mean predicted probability", ylab = "observed rate of >$50K",
     main = "Reliability curve")
lines(cal_lr$mean_predicted, cal_lr$actual_rate, type = "b", pch = 17, lwd = 2,
      col = "#b03030")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
legend("topleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.85,
       legend = c("naiveBayes", "logistic regression", "perfect calibration"),
       col = c("#20607a", "#b03030", "grey40"),
       pch = c(19, 17, NA), lty = c(1, 1, 2))

col_nb <- rgb(32 / 255, 96 / 255, 122 / 255, alpha = 0.60)
col_lr <- rgb(176 / 255, 48 / 255, 48 / 255, alpha = 0.50)

hist(prob_nb, breaks = 40, col = col_nb, border = NA,
     xlab = "predicted P(income > $50K)", ylab = "count",
     main = "Where the predicted probabilities pile up")
hist(prob_lr, breaks = 40, col = col_lr, border = NA, add = TRUE)
legend("top", bty = "n", cex = 0.85, fill = c(col_nb, col_lr),
       legend = c("naiveBayes", "logistic regression"))

par(op)
```

Look at the right-hand histogram. Naive Bayes tends to pile predictions against 0 and 1
while logistic regression spreads them through the middle. That is the double-counting of
correlated evidence, visible directly.

The Brier score measures calibration and accuracy together — lower is better:

```{r adult-brier, eval=have_e1071}
brier <- function(p, y) mean((p - y)^2)
cat(sprintf("naiveBayes:          %.4f\n", brier(prob_nb, y_test_num)))
cat(sprintf("logistic regression: %.4f\n", brier(prob_lr, y_test_num)))
```

**The practical rule:** use Naive Bayes probabilities to *rank* cases, not as calibrated
risk estimates. If you need the number itself to mean something — "this person has a 30%
chance" — recalibrate (isotonic regression via `stats::isoreg`, or Platt scaling by
fitting a `glm` of the outcome on the model's log-odds) or use a method that estimates
probabilities properly.

## 3.10 Who does the model fail?

An aggregate metric hides distributional damage. A model can look fine overall and be
systematically worse for a subgroup. The features here include `sex` and `race`, so we can
and should check.

This is a descriptive audit, not a fairness verdict — "fairness" has several mutually
incompatible formal definitions, and choosing among them is an ethical and political
question a document like this does not settle.

```{r adult-subgroups, eval=have_e1071}
subgroup_report <- function(attribute, truth, pred, data, positive = ">50K") {
  grp <- data[[attribute]]
  out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(droplevels(factor(grp))), function(lev) {
    k <- grp == lev
    t_k <- truth[k]; p_k <- pred[k]
    pos <- t_k == positive
    neg <- !pos
    data.frame(
      group          = lev,
      n              = sum(k),
      true_rate      = mean(pos),
      predicted_rate = mean(p_k == positive),
      recall         = if (any(pos)) mean(p_k[pos] == positive) else NA_real_,
      FPR            = if (any(neg)) mean(p_k[neg] == positive) else NA_real_,
      accuracy       = mean(t_k == p_k),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  }))
  out[order(-out$n), ]
}

cat("=== by sex ", strrep("=", 50), "\n")
print(format(subgroup_report("sex", test$income, pred_nb, test), digits = 3),
      row.names = FALSE)

cat("\n=== by race ", strrep("=", 49), "\n")
print(format(subgroup_report("race", test$income, pred_nb, test), digits = 3),
      row.names = FALSE)
```

Compare the `recall` column across groups. Recall is the share of genuinely high-earning
people the model finds. If it is markedly lower for one group, the model disproportionately
fails to identify high earners in that group — and if such a model were used to target a
programme or allocate a resource, that gap would become a distributional harm.

Two mechanisms usually drive this, and they call for different responses:

- **Base rates differ across groups.** Naive Bayes multiplies in `P(sex | class)`, so a
  group with a lower observed rate of high earnings is pushed toward the low-income
  prediction for that reason alone.
- **Sample size differs.** Smaller groups have noisier likelihood estimates, and Laplace
  smoothing pulls them harder toward uniform (adding 1 to a denominator of 200 matters
  more than adding 1 to a denominator of 20,000).

Worth trying: refit without `sex` and `race` and see what happens to the gaps. Removing a
protected attribute often does **not** close them, because correlated features such as
`occupation` and `relationship` carry the same information. "Fairness through unawareness"
mostly does not work, and this dataset shows it cleanly.

## 3.11 What would we conclude?

Stated as a researcher would state it:

> Using twelve demographic and employment characteristics from the 1994 CPS, a Naive Bayes
> classifier separates individuals earning above and below \$50,000 substantially better
> than chance, and comparably to logistic regression, despite strongly violated
> independence assumptions among its predictors. Educational credentials and occupational
> category carry the largest evidence weights, in an ordering consistent with
> stratification research. The model's probability estimates are poorly calibrated,
> concentrating near 0 and 1; they are usable for ranking but not as risk estimates.
> Recall varies across sex and racial groups, reflecting differences in both base rates and
> estimation precision.

What it does **not** license:

- No causal claim. Nothing here establishes that a credential *causes* higher earnings.
- No claim about today. These are 1994 associations at a 1994 dollar threshold.
- No claim about the population without weights. `fnlwgt` exists for a reason and we
  ignored it, as nearly everyone using this dataset does. A published analysis should not.

---

# Closing

## Choosing an approach in R

- All predictors are factors → `e1071::naiveBayes()` handles it directly.
- Continuous predictors, plausibly normal within class → leave them numeric and
  `naiveBayes()` fits a Gaussian per class.
- Continuous but clearly not normal → bin with `cut()`, as we did for `capital_gain`, or
  use `klaR::NaiveBayes(usekernel = TRUE)` for kernel density estimates.
- Text or count data → `naivebayes::multinomial_naive_bayes()`.

## Mistakes that cost people marks and papers

1. **Forgetting `stringsAsFactors`.** Since R 4.0 your character columns are not factors.
   Convert explicitly and `stopifnot()` it.
2. **Letting an integer-coded category stay numeric.** `naiveBayes()` fits a Gaussian to
   it without comment. It runs. It is wrong.
3. **Not knowing which smoothing you got.** `laplace` defaults to 0 at fit time;
   `threshold` defaults to 0.001 at predict time. Two knobs, two defaults, and neither is
   mentioned in most tutorials.
4. **Mismatched factor levels in `newdata`.** Build prediction rows from
   `levels(train$col)`, never from bare strings.
5. **Reading `m$apriori` as probabilities.** They are counts; use `prop.table()`.
6. **Reading `m$tables` with the wrong orientation.** Rows are classes, columns are
   levels — the transpose of what `prop.table(table(x, y), 2)` gives you.
7. **Reporting accuracy on imbalanced data.** Always put the majority-class baseline
   beside it.
8. **Treating the probabilities as calibrated.** Rank with them; do not quote them.
9. **Reading a likelihood ratio as a causal effect.** It is a marginal association with
   nothing held constant.
10. **Including two features that encode the same thing** (`education` and
    `education_num`). Multiplying likelihoods counts that evidence twice.

## R and Python: the same model, opposite defaults

| | `e1071::naiveBayes` | `sklearn.CategoricalNB` |
|---|---|---|
| Smoothing default | `laplace = 0` — none | `alpha = 1.0` — add-one |
| Reproduces the slides out of the box? | Yes | No |
| Zero likelihoods at predict time | patched to `threshold = 0.001` | left as 0 |
| Categorical encoding | automatic from factors | you must encode to integers |
| Numeric columns | Gaussian, chosen automatically | you pick the class |

The most useful thing on that table is the first row. If you port an analysis between the
two languages and the numbers move by a few percent, this is the first place to look.

## Exercises

1. In Example 2, add a fourth predictor of your own invention to the 14 rows and see how
   far the posterior for the test case moves. How many predictors can 14 rows support?
2. Re-run section 3.10 after dropping `sex` and `race` from `CAT`. Does the subgroup recall
   gap close? Explain what you find.
3. Sweep `laplace` over the Adult data as we did for the 14-row dataset. Why is the curve
   so much flatter?
4. Replace the `age_band` and `hours_band` cut points with equal-width bins
   (`cut(x, breaks = 6)`) and then with deciles
   (`cut(x, quantile(x, seq(0, 1, 0.1)), include.lowest = TRUE)`). How much does AUC move?
   What does that tell you about how much the binning choice mattered?
5. Load `adult.test` (same URL with `.test`, but skip the first line and strip the trailing
   period from the labels), and use it as a held-out set instead of splitting `adult.data`.
   Do the metrics change? Why might a pre-defined split be preferable to your own?
6. Implement Platt scaling: fit `glm(y ~ log_odds, family = binomial())` on a validation
   split, where `log_odds` comes from the Naive Bayes probabilities. Does the Brier score
   improve? Does AUC change, and why not?
